newsitem.title: USA: N.Y.C. Mayor sees crime down, critics see overtime.
newsitem.headline: N.Y.C. Mayor sees crime down, critics see overtime.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani on Monday, saying he had reversed "one failure after another" after taking office, hailed his successes, including lower crime, cleaner streets and fewer people on welfare.

His critics, however, were equally swift to point to what they saw as disturbing trends, such as poor planning for overtime expenditures, a drop in patrol strength by the police and rising numbers of children who need help.

The mayor, who released his report on how city agencies performed during fiscal year 1996 at a public meeting at City Hall, also pointed to New York City's new success at attracting businesses and improving public hospitals.

The city, which lost a number of Fortune 500 companies during the past 25 years, now has become a place that companies, like Disney, which is developing a project in midtown's Times Square, want to invest in, he said.

Since the start of 1994, 47,944 private jobs were retained, almost double the number achieved by former Mayor David Dinkins, a Democrat, during his four years, said Giuliani, who is a Republican. He said his Administration created more than 100,000 jobs, adding that recapturing the movie and television business, which had been threatening to shoot elsewhere, also was boosting tourism.

Another area he highlighted was an 18.6 percent drop in the murder rate from January to September 1996, noting that more than 36 percent of the national drop in crime indexes over the past two calender years was due to New York City.

Saying that his predecessor projected the number of people on welfare might rise as high as 1.4 million, Giuliani said that as of August 31, 1996, the rolls stood at 995,000. The 14.3 percent drop was attributed to stiffer evaluations and a a new workfare program.
The mayor also defended a sharp rise in "fair hearings" requested by recipients who had their benefits cut off, saying this was due to stricter checks on who was eligibile.
The city's streets now are cleaner, Giuliani added, saying that in June and July there were no districts rated dirty for the first time since October 1987.

The mayor, who repeatedly referred to the failure of the previous Administration to plan for rising welfare rolls and promised to try to soften the effect of a new federal welfare bill, said other problems also were left to him to solve.
"We have a lot of roads to reconstruct, a lot of bridges to rebuild, and a lot of tunnels to fix."
Peter Vallone, D-Queens, who is the Speaker of the City Council, in prepared remarks questioned some of the mayor's findings about how the police department was doing.

Saying a drop in the Police Department's patrol strength was "particularly disturbing," Vallone added "This is not what we were led to expect when we were promised more cops on the streets after the merger." In April 1995, the city's police force merged with the Transit and Housing police.

A city official noted the data include 1,500 police recruits who have yet to hit the streets, while Giuliani focused on the overall drop in crime as the best measure of success, despite his emphasis on increasing patrol strength early this year.
The city's difficulty in planning for overtime also drew the Speaker's fire. In fiscal year 1996, it rose $21.7 million to $493 million, but only was budgeted at $354 million.

And the Administration had said that "operational overtime," excluding winter storms and other unpredictable events, had fallen. In fiscal 1997, which began on July 1, the overtime budget is $296 million.

Finally, the Speaker noted the new agency, the Administration for Child Services, is seeing "dramatic growth in its caseloads and vowed to hold the Giuliani Administration to its promises to improve this area.
